title: Fare and surge pricing strategies
idea: Pricing in a cab system is two swappable strategies: a `FareStrategy` per vehicle type computes the base fare, and a `SurgePolicy` scales it by current demand.
points: This is the Strategy pattern from c08: one interface, one class per pricing rule.
A map keyed by `VehicleType` picks the fare rule; adding XL needs no `if`.
Surge is a separate policy, so cities can change surge without touching fares.
Keep money in `long` cents; round each fractional product once, never cents already rounded.

hero.title: One sedan quote through the pricing steps

steps.caption: The caller builds a `TripInfo` record: vehicle type, distance and minutes. It holds no pricing logic.
The calculator looks up the `FareStrategy` registered for SEDAN. A missing type fails with a clear message.
`MeteredFare` adds flag fall, 5 km at 90 and 12 minutes at 20: 840 cents.
840 is above the sedan minimum of 500, so the minimum leaves it unchanged.
25 open requests over 20 free drivers is 1.25. `DemandSurge` rounds down to a 0.25 step and caps it.
The calculator multiplies once and rounds once: 1050 cents.

code.title: The problem: one if-else
code.caption: Every rule lives in one method, so each new type or surge rule is an edit with new bugs.

walk.text: One static method owns all vehicle types and surge. It violates the Open/Closed Principle (OCP).
The bike branch never applies surge. Nobody decided that; the branch was just forgotten.
Surge is a boolean and a fixed doubling. A city that wants 1.5x must edit this line.
XL was added to the enum but not here, so it fails only at runtime.
The enum and the pricing method change for the same reason but live apart.

code.title: The fix: two strategies
code.caption: Fare rules and surge rules are separate strategies, injected into one small calculator.

walk.text: Two narrow interfaces. `SurgePolicy` has one method, so a lambda can implement it.
One record covers every metered rule; the data differs per type, not the code.
Ratio rounded down to 0.25 steps, floored at 1 and capped. Zero drivers means maximum surge.
`Map.copyOf` freezes the rates, so callers cannot change prices after construction.
Multiply the base by surge and round that product once; never re-round earlier results.
Wiring happens in one place. A new city gets a new map or policy, not new code.
The bike hop is under its minimum, so it is raised first, then surged.

pitfalls: Using `double` for money collects rounding errors across steps; store cents in `long`.
Applying surge before the minimum fare under-charges short trips; fix and document the order.
Reading demand inside `FareStrategy` mixes two concerns; pass it to a separate `SurgePolicy`.

quiz.q: Same classes as the fix. What does this print?
quiz.why: Metered is 150 + 180 + 100 = 430, raised to the 500 minimum. 11/10 is 1.1, which rounds down to the 1.00 step.

takeaway: Fare rule per vehicle, surge rule per market, both injected strategies.
